title: Sound
starter: Sound is a smooth wave, but computers store numbers. Suggest how a recording could be turned into numbers, and what is lost.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Analogue to digital
facts: Sound is an analogue wave: it changes smoothly and continuously.
Computers store discrete numbers, so the wave must be measured at intervals.
Each measurement is called a sample, and is stored in binary.
stations.challenge: Why can't a computer store a sound wave exactly?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Sound is an analogue wave: it changes smoothly and continuously.
Also credit: Computers store discrete numbers, so the wave must be measured at intervals.

questions.a: Measuring the amplitude of a sound wave at regular intervals and storing each measurement in binary

questions.q: Place a sample in each column, at the level nearest the wave.
questions.a: One sample per column at the level nearest the wave (8 × 3 = 24 bits)

stations.name: Sample rate
facts: Sample rate is the number of samples taken per second, measured in hertz.
A higher rate follows the wave more closely, so the recording is more accurate.
stations.challenge: What happens to the recording if the sample rate is too low?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Sample rate is the number of samples taken per second, measured in hertz.
Also credit: A higher rate follows the wave more closely, so the recording is more accurate.

questions.a: How many samples are taken each second

questions.q: What is the effect of doubling the sample rate?
questions.a: Better quality, and twice the file size

stations.name: Bit depth
facts: Bit depth is the number of bits used to store each sample.
More bits means more possible levels, so the amplitude is recorded more precisely.
stations.challenge: How many levels does a bit depth of 4 give?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Bit depth is the number of bits used to store each sample.
Also credit: More bits means more possible levels, so the amplitude is recorded more precisely.

questions.q: This time the bit depth is 4, giving 16 levels. Place each sample at the nearest level.
questions.a: One sample per column at the level nearest the wave (8 × 4 = 32 bits)

questions.q: What is the effect of increasing the bit depth?
questions.a: Each sample is recorded more precisely, and the file gets bigger

stations.name: Sound file size
facts: File size (bits) = sample rate × bit depth × duration in seconds.
Double any one of them and the file size doubles.
Stereo doubles it again, because each channel is stored separately.
stations.challenge: Calculate the size of 10 seconds at 8,000 Hz with 8-bit samples.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: File size (bits) = sample rate × bit depth × duration in seconds.
Also credit: Double any one of them and the file size doubles.

questions.q: A 30-second clip is sampled at 44,100 Hz with a bit depth of 16. What is its size in bits?
Which change would halve a sound file's size?

stations.name: Quality against size
facts: Higher sample rate and bit depth mean better quality and bigger files.
Speech needs far less than music, so phone calls use low rates.
Choose what's good enough for the purpose.
stations.challenge: Why is a phone call sampled at a much lower rate than a music track?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Higher sample rate and bit depth mean better quality and bigger files.
Also credit: Speech needs far less than music, so phone calls use low rates.

questions.q: Why do phone calls use a low sample rate?
questions.a: Speech is still clear, and the smaller files are quicker to transmit

questions.q: Which combination gives the highest quality recording?
questions.a: A high sample rate and a high bit depth

stations.name: In the studio
facts: Practise reading a wave and choosing the nearest level at each sample.
Then calculate the file size from your choices.
This is exactly what an exam question on sound representation looks like.
stations.challenge: Complete both sampling tasks on your worksheet.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Practise reading a wave and choosing the nearest level at each sample.
Also credit: Then calculate the file size from your choices.

questions.q: Sample this wave. It rises and falls twice, so look carefully.
questions.a: One sample per column at the level nearest the wave (8 × 3 = 24 bits)

questions.q: A sample is stored with 3 bits. What is the highest level it can record?

final.name: Final challenge: sample and calculate

questions.q: Place each sample at the level nearest the wave.
questions.a: One sample per column at the level nearest the wave (8 × 3 = 24 bits)

questions.q: A 60-second recording is sampled at 20,000 Hz with a bit depth of 8. What is the file size in bytes?
The same recording is made in stereo. What happens to the file size?
questions.a: It doubles, because each channel is stored separately

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Describe what happens when a sound wave is sampled.
points: Sound is an analogue wave: it changes smoothly and continuously.
This is exactly what an exam question on sound representation looks like.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
